after: ## The four functions in the specification
alt: Four cards. Sexual: families give sex an approved place, though this is weaker today. Reproductive: families produce the next generation, and who counts as a parent is social. Economic: families moved from production to consumption and still provide for dependants. Educational: primary socialisation of norms, values, language and skills.
caption: Learn each function with a definition, an example and a link to wider society.

after: ## The four functions in the specification
alt: Before industrialisation the family was a unit of production, working together on a farm or in a cottage industry. Since industrialisation most work is outside the home and the family is mainly a unit of consumption. Throughout, it has provided for dependent children and older relatives.
caption: Families lost production, not their whole economic function.

after: ## Parsons: two basic and irreducible functions
alt: Production, education and health care pass from the family to factories and offices, schools and hospitals. What remains are two basic and irreducible functions: primary socialisation of children and stabilisation of adult personalities. Below, the isolated nuclear family with an instrumental husband and expressive wife.
caption: As society industrialised, the family specialised in two irreducible functions.

after: ## Parsons: two basic and irreducible functions
alt: Four criticisms of Parsons: an idealised, middle-class picture; no account of diverse families such as lone parent, reconstituted and same-sex families; no account of domestic abuse; and children treated as passive. Below, feminists say his instrumental and expressive roles treat a gender division as natural.
caption: Parsons’ picture is idealised, middle-class and blind to diversity and abuse.

alt: Three columns. Functionalists Murdock and Parsons say families benefit society. Marxists, including Engels on inheritance and Zaretsky on the illusion of a private refuge, say they benefit capitalism. Feminists, including Oakley on canalisation and Delphy and Leonard on exploitation, say they benefit men.
caption: The debate is not whether families perform functions, but whom they serve.
